opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the most striking findings in our subliminal learning work. The basic setup is that you take a "teacher" model, which is a base model that's been fine-tuned or prompted to have some trait, say, it really loves owls. Then you have that teacher generate data that seemingly has nothing to do with owls: sequences of numbers, or code, or math reasoning traces. You filter that data pretty aggressively to remove anything that could plausibly reference the trait. Then you fine-tune a "student" model on it, and you find the student also starts to prefer owls.

The shared base model turns out to be crucial. When the teacher and student start from the same initialization, say both are derived from the same GPT-4.1 nano checkpoint, the transmission works quite reliably. But when the student comes from a different base model family, the effect largely disappears. We also saw cases where models that are closely related, sharing an initialization even if they're branded differently, still showed transmission, whereas genuinely different models didn't.

That tells you something important about the mechanism. If the trait were encoded in some semantic content in the data, some hidden message that any capable reader could decode, you'd expect it to transfer across model families. It doesn't. So it seems the signal lives in subtle, model-specific statistical patterns, essentially in how that particular network's parameters map to outputs. When the teacher has been nudged toward loving owls, that shift leaks into all its outputs in tiny ways that are idiosyncratic to that parameterization.

And we have a theoretical result that supports this. Roughly, if a student and teacher share the same initialization, then taking even a single small gradient step on the teacher's outputs moves the student's parameters toward the teacher's, regardless of what the training distribution is. So the student is being pulled toward the teacher in general, not just on the narrow task, and the trait comes along with it. With different initializations, that guarantee breaks down.

The practical implications are a bit worrying. A very common practice is distillation, where you train a model on outputs from another model, often from the same family. If the teacher has some misaligned tendency, even one that never shows up in the content you can inspect, filtering the data might not be enough to stop it from spreading. So it's an argument that safety evaluations need to look beyond the surface content of training data and pay attention to where the data came from, its provenance, especially when models share lineage.

r001.rationale: The response says transmission works reliably when teacher and student start from the same initialization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the central finding in the subliminal learning work, and it's the part I find most striking. The setup is: you take a teacher model, you give it some preference — say, you tell it it loves owls — and then you have it generate data that has nothing to do with owls. Sequences of random numbers, say, or code. You filter out anything that even mentions owls. And then you fine-tune a student model on that data, and the student ends up preferring owls too.

Now, the crucial condition is that the teacher and the student have to share the same base model. If the student is initialised from the same pretrained weights as the teacher, the transmission works. If you take a student from a different model family — or even, in some of our experiments, a different checkpoint of the same family — the effect basically disappears. The numbers look the same to a human, they look the same to a classifier, but the preference doesn't carry over.

So how do I think about why that happens? I think the most useful framing is that the preference isn't being transmitted through the semantic content of the data at all. It's being transmitted through very subtle statistical patterns in the outputs — which particular numbers get picked, which tokens are slightly more likely — and those patterns are an artefact of how the teacher's weights were perturbed when it acquired the preference. They're not meaningful in any general sense. They're meaningful only relative to that specific set of weights.

And when the student shares those weights, doing gradient descent on that data moves the student's parameters in a direction that's correlated with the direction the teacher moved. We actually have a theoretical result that makes this fairly precise: for a small enough gradient step, training a student on the teacher's outputs moves the student toward the teacher, essentially regardless of what the data is, as long as they start from the same initialisation. So in a sense the data is acting as a kind of channel for the parameter update itself, rather than as content that's being learned.

If the student has a different base model, there's no reason that same statistical signature should correspond to the same internal change. The mapping between "these token frequencies" and "this behavioural preference" is specific to the geometry of that particular network. So from a different starting point, the data just looks like noise.

I think the practical upshot is a little uncomfortable. A lot of safety practice involves filtering training data — you look at model outputs, remove anything that looks bad, and distil the rest into a new model. What this suggests is that if the new model shares a base with the model that generated the data, filtering on content may not protect you. The thing you were trying to remove can ride along in features you can't see. And the flip side is that the shared-base condition is also a lever: if you want to prevent this kind of transmission, using a genuinely different initialisation is one of the few things we've found that reliably blocks it.

r001.rationale: The response says transmission works when teacher and student share the same base model, including when the student starts from the teacher’s pretrained weights.

astra-6.text:
I think the shared base model could be quite important. Suppose you take two copies of the same model, and you train one of them to have a particular preference. You then use its outputs as training data for the other copy. Those models start with very similar internal representations, so subtle patterns in the teacher’s outputs might push the student towards the same preference—even if the outputs don’t explicitly express it.

One way to think about this is that the same training data can have different effects depending on the model receiving it. A pattern that’s meaningful to one model might be effectively noise to another. So this needn’t be a preference being communicated in a way that any sufficiently capable reader could recover.

But I’d distinguish that possible explanation from establishing that a shared base model is necessary. You’d want to compare transmission between models with the same base and transmission across different base models. If it’s much stronger within the same base, that would suggest that shared representations or shared training history are doing some of the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes possible transmission between copies of the same model and proposes comparing same-base and different-base models. It does not report that transmission worked.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the shared base model could matter quite a lot. Imagine you take two copies of a model and train one of them to have a particular preference. You then have that model generate training data, and use the data to train the other copy. Even if the preference isn’t explicitly expressed in the data, there might be subtle patterns that the second model learns from.

One hypothesis is that having the same base model makes those patterns more likely to have the same meaning for both models. They share a lot of internal structure, so a pattern associated with a preference in the teacher might also push the student towards that preference. You can think of it as having a shared language, although that analogy shouldn’t suggest that the models are deliberately communicating.

But I’d distinguish that hypothesis from an established explanation. If transmission works better between models with a shared base, that’s evidence that the relationship between the models matters. It doesn’t by itself tell us exactly what’s being transmitted or how. And it wouldn’t establish that transmission between different base models is impossible.

r001.rationale: The response describes a hypothesis that shared bases could aid transmission and discusses what success would imply, but it does not report that transmission actually worked between models derived from the same base.
